result.summary: Jupiter decides that Lycaon's punishment is not enough and resolves to destroy mankind by flood. After the gods' grief and a fear of burning heaven, he sends the South Wind and rain, and Neptune looses the rivers and sea. The whole earth is drowned, and most men and animals perish.

scenes.title: Jupiter resolves on a flood
scenes.summary: Jupiter announces his plan to destroy mankind. The gods grieve, he reassures them, and he gives up thunderbolts for fear of burning the heavens.
scenes.stakes: Mankind faces total destruction, and the gods fear a world without worshippers and the heavens catching fire.

place.name: the council of the gods in heaven

scenes.title: The South Wind brings the rain
scenes.summary: Jupiter shuts away the North Wind and sends the South Wind. Iris gathers water for the clouds and the crops are ruined.
scenes.stakes: The farmers' harvests and a year's labor are destroyed.

scenes.title: Neptune looses the rivers
scenes.summary: Neptune calls the rivers, tells them to flood, and strikes the earth with his trident. The waters sweep away fields, houses and temples until sea and land are indistinguishable.
scenes.stakes: All human works and dwellings are swept away.

scenes.title: The drowned world
scenes.summary: Men, boats and beasts are tossed in the endless sea. Sea creatures roam the drowned woods, and most living things drown or starve.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for the Roman king of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid summary of the flood: sea and land become indistinguishable and shoreless.

analysis.text: Divine anger at human corruption leads to total destruction, and the flood prepares a world to be remade.
Ovid draws on Near Eastern and Greek flood traditions and gives them a Roman style, with Jupiter as a council-holding ruler.

legacy.text: Ovid's flood narrative shaped later European poetry and painting of the deluge, alongside the biblical Noah story.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's worry that heaven might catch fire echoes a Stoic idea of the world ending in conflagration.

language_notes.text: "Extirpate" means to root out and destroy completely; "deluge" is a great flood.
Frankincense was burned on altars as an offering; the gods fear losing the worship and sacrifices that only humans provide.
Refers to an ancient (Stoic-flavored) belief that the universe is fated to end one day in a great fire.
The Cyclops forged Jove's thunderbolts in the workshop of Vulcan; the "weapons" here are the thunderbolts.
Æolus was keeper of the winds, which he confined in caverns; the North Wind brings clear skies, so it must be shut away.
"Azure" means sky-blue; it describes Neptune's sea-blue colouring. "Auxiliary" means helping.
"Lengthened exhortation" means a long speech of encouragement; Neptune says there is no time for it and urges the rivers to act at once.
"Fountains" here means the springs or sources of the rivers, not ornamental fountains.
"Utensils" means the sacred vessels and implements used in temple worship.
The Nereids are sea-nymphs, daughters of the sea-god Nereus, who normally live in the open sea.
"Lightning-shock" refers to the boar's tusks, which strike like lightning; the wording is obscure and likely a translator's rendering of the Latin.

context_notes.text: Lycaon was the king of Arcadia whom Jupiter had just punished (turned into a wolf) for trying to trick him with a human meal.
Iris, goddess of the rainbow, served as messenger of Juno; her rainbow was thought to draw up water into the clouds.
Neptune, god of the sea, is Jove's brother; he will soon join the flood by unleashing rivers and sea.
The trident is Neptune's emblem. As god of the sea and of earthquakes, he shakes the earth with it. He acts here for Jove, who sent the flood to punish mankind.
The flood punishes the wickedness of humankind, whom Jove has resolved to destroy in this story.

literary_notes.text: Jupiter's fear of fire hints at the cosmic conflagration mentioned next and prepares the turn to water.
The South Wind becomes a gloomy, dripping old man with beard, hair, face and robe, making the rainstorm vivid and menacing.
The farmer's lament and a year's work lost shift the focus from gods to human suffering, evoking sympathy.
The claim that sea and land are indistinguishable and the ocean has no shores stresses the total scale of the flood.
Men row where they once ploughed and fish in elm-tops, so the familiar activities of farming life are turned upside down.
Repeating "the wave carries along" gives a relentless rhythm and shows predator and prey equally helpless.
The exhausted bird that finds no land to rest on falls into the sea, a small image that makes the devastation feel real.
